name: Circulation of the blood
note: Not that blood moves, but that it circulates: same blood returns to the heart, not consumed, and the quantity is small enough that arterial blood must reach veins via capillaries

name: Lung gas exchange
note: How the lungs work: air does not simply soak into the blood like water into a sponge. Oxygen and carbon dioxide pass across a very thin barrier between the air sacs of the lung and the blood vessels around them, oxygen going into the blood and carbon dioxide out. It needs the understanding of circulation and a microscope to see the fine structures. Knowing this explains how breathing fails in lung disease.

name: Digestive process
note: How food is turned into the body's materials. Digestion is not only mechanical grinding: acid in the stomach and ferments (enzymes, chemicals that speed up reactions) in the gut break food down chemically, and the products are absorbed through the intestinal wall into the blood. It needs a microscope and chemical analysis to study the juices. This lets a physician see why some foods nourish and why some illnesses prevent absorption.

name: Nervous system structure and function
note: Not simple mechanical tubes but specialized tissue conducting electrical signals; distinction between sensory and motor nerves

name: Endocrine glands and hormones
note: Distinction between nervous (electrical) and endocrine (chemical) signaling; hormones as circulating chemical messengers

name: Kidney filtration
note: How the kidneys make urine. They do not simply sieve the blood: they filter a large volume and then selectively take back the useful substances and, as needed, the water, leaving waste to leave the body. This lets the body keep its water and salt balanced. It needs the knowledge of circulation and a microscope to see the tiny filtering units. Knowing it explains kidney failure and swelling.

name: Immune system and antibodies
note: How the body defends itself against specific infections. Each kind of germ provokes its own antibodies (proteins that attack that germ), and a second exposure produces a faster, stronger response, which is why survivors of some diseases are protected. It needs germ theory and a microscope. It is the basis of vaccination and of understanding why some people never catch a disease twice.

name: Cell as basic unit of life
note: Not just observation of cells under lens, but the theory that organisation is cellular throughout, not fibrous or humoral

name: Mendelian inheritance laws
note: The laws of inheritance found by breeding experiments: traits are passed on as separate particles, not blended like paint. Some traits are dominant (they show when present) and others recessive (they hide unless inherited from both parents), giving predictable ratios such as three to one, and nine to three to three to one, in the offspring of crosses. It needs a garden plot or breeding stock and many seasons of careful counts.

name: Chromosome and heredity
note: The threadlike structures inside cells that carry the hereditary material. They can be seen under a microscope when a cell divides, in the ordinary division (mitosis) and the special division that makes eggs and sperm (meiosis). Tracking which traits travel together lets researchers map genes to places on chromosomes. It needs Mendelian ratios and a good microscope with stains.

name: Gene as unit of inheritance
note: The unit of inheritance, understood not as a passive bead on a string but as an active agent: each gene directs the making of one enzyme (one gene, one enzyme). A mutation is a change in a gene, which changes what it makes. It needs the chromosome theory and breeding experiments. It explains inherited diseases and how new traits appear.

name: DNA as hereditary material
note: DNA, the molecule that carries heredity. It is a double helix (two strands wound round each other) whose rungs are pairs of chemical bases; the information lies in the order of the bases, and base pairing lets each strand be copied accurately when cells divide. It needs the concept of the gene and good chemistry, including atoms and elements, to isolate and analyse it.

name: Stethoscope
note: Laennec's tube: stiffened paper initially, then wood; acoustic coupling transforms inaudible vibrations to audible without stethoscope being nearly as gross as hands on chest

name: Percussion technique
note: A method of examining a patient's chest or abdomen by tapping on it with the fingers and listening to the note. The sound is dull over fluid or solid tissue and hollow over air, so a trained ear can locate fluid in the lung or an enlarged organ. It was introduced by Auenbrugger. It needs no equipment, but it takes long training and practice to tell the notes apart.

name: Systematic auscultation
note: Listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope and systematically cataloguing them: crackles (rales), wheezes and rumbles (rhonchi), murmurs and clicks of the heart. The point is to match each sound to the disease found at autopsy, and so to give a diagnosis and a prognosis. It needs the stethoscope and many cases to learn the patterns.

name: Clinical thermometer
note: Mercury in glass with fixed point at 37 C. Temperature tells severity of infection. Fever is sometimes the body fighting infection.

name: Sphygmomanometer
note: Riva-Rocci cuff and column: cuff inflated until radial pulse disappears, pressure read from mercury manometer, deflation to systolic and diastolic points

name: Ophthalmoscope
kb: Instrument for direct visualization of retina and optic disc
note: Helmholtz's coaxial light path: light source and observer on same axis; mirror with central hole; correct focus requires interpretation

name: Otoscope
note: An instrument for looking into the ear: a small cone (speculum) holds the ear canal open while a lens and a light let the doctor see the eardrum. It teaches recognition of wax (cerumen), infection, a perforated drum and the normal reflection of light on the drum. It needs ground lenses and a light source. Without good light and training, a doctor misreads what he sees.

name: Laryngoscope
note: A laryngoscope lets a doctor see the throat above the vocal cords. In the indirect form a small angled mirror on a long handle is held at the back of the mouth, while light from a lamp or a head mirror is reflected down the throat, and the doctor sees the vocal cords in the mirror. It needs a good light source and a small mirror, and it makes the voice box visible for diagnosis. Direct views for anaesthesia came later.

name: Rigid endoscope
note: Early versions for urethra and bladder; later gastroscopy; achromatic objective required; light source separate initially, then coaxial

name: Cystoscope
note: An instrument for looking inside the bladder: a thin rigid tube (a rigid endoscope) with a light and a lens is passed up the urethra. A sheath with openings carries a working channel through which small instruments can be passed. The doctor sees the lining of the bladder and the openings of the ureters (the tubes from the kidneys) directly. It needs a rigid endoscope and fine metalwork.

name: X-ray radiography
note: X-ray tube, transformer for high voltage, cooling, filtration for soft rays, photographic plate exposure time; fluoroscopy followed

name: Fluoroscopy imaging
note: Barium sulfate fluorescence visible in dark; lead glass shielding; carbon arc or tungsten target; image intensification came much later

name: Contrast media
note: Barium swallow for GI tract; urography for urinary system; early iodine compounds for angiography; toxicity and allergic reaction gradually recognized
_internal: [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

name: Electrocardiogram
note: String galvanometer initially; three standard bipolar leads; later six unipolar; PQRST waves; arrhythmias and ischemia visible

name: Electroencephalogram
note: Scalp electrodes; low voltage millivolt signals require vacuum tube amplification; alpha waves at rest; seizure spikes; sleep stages

name: Basal metabolic rate measurement
note: Measured during fasting sleep; oxygen consumption or carbon dioxide production; thyroid function assessment; reproducibility requires strict conditions

name: Haemocytometer
note: A haemocytometer is a thick glass slide with a grid of fine lines etched in it, forming a chamber of exactly known depth. A blood sample is diluted by a known amount and placed in the chamber, and the cells are counted under a microscope in a few of the squares. Because the volume counted is known, the count gives the number of cells per volume of blood, which shows conditions such as anaemia. The grid must be ruled very accurately.

name: Differential white cell count
note: Blood smear stained and examined under oil immersion; neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils; left shift in infection

name: Urinalysis
note: Specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin; crystals and casts under microscope; infection indicated by bacteria and white cells

name: Blood glucose measurement
note: Fasting baseline; response to glucose load; distinction between diabetes and hypoglycemia; Somogyi effect and brittle diabetes

name: Wassermann test
note: Antibodies in syphilitic serum fix complement; addition of sensitized RBC shows hemolysis or lack thereof; false positives in lupus and atypical pneumonia

name: Tuberculin test
kb: Intradermal injection of tuberculin to detect TB sensitization
note: Mantoux test: intradermal injection of purified protein derivative; delayed hypersensitivity reaction; induration size interpretation; active vs latent TB

name: Tissue biopsy
note: Needle or punch biopsy; immediate fixation; staining and microscopy; diagnosis of malignancy, inflammation, infection without surgical exploration

name: Frozen section histology
note: Specimen frozen in cryostat at -20 C; thin sections cut without embedding; rapid staining; intraoperative diagnosis for tumor margins and unexpected findings

name: Autoclave sterilizer
note: Prevost and Junker's pressure vessel; 120 C at 2 atmospheres; spore kill vs vegetative cell; correct loading and cycles critical

name: Surgical glove
note: Halsted's gloves: latex not yet vulcanized properly so degraded; talc powder inside for donning; protective not just of patient but of surgeon

name: Surgical facemask
note: Initially cloth; later gauze in layers; protection of surgical field from oral and nasal flora; not protection of wearer

name: Surgical gown
note: Initially ordinary cotton; later white linen for visibility of blood; design prevents microbial shedding from body; sleeves fully extended

name: Sterile drape
note: Sterile cloths laid over the patient so that only the operative site is exposed. Towels and sheets are arranged in layers, with a hole (fenestration) over the site, and their edges are kept from wicking germs inward from unsterile surfaces. It needs clean linen, boiling or steaming to sterilise it, and a disciplined team. A single non-sterile touch undoes it.

name: Catgut suture
note: Not cat but sheep or horse; prepared from submucosa; caliber standardization; chromic acid treatment for slower absorption

name: Synthetic suture
note: Stitching thread made of nylon monofilament (a single smooth strand). It causes less inflammation than catgut, a thread made from animal gut, and it does not dissolve, so it holds for as long as needed. It needs a chemical industry that can make nylon and draw it fine. Surgical silk is still used for special purposes. A thread that never dissolves must be removed or left in permanently.

name: Surgical haemostat
note: A surgical clamp for gripping a bleeding vessel to stop blood loss. It has two serrated jaws, a spring handle and a ratchet that locks it shut, so the surgeon's hands are free. Designs such as the Pean, the Kelly and the small mosquito suit large and small vessels, and teeth hold arteries (high pressure) or veins. It needs good springy steel and a machine shop to cut the ratchet precisely.

name: Self-retaining retractor
note: A surgical instrument that holds a wound open without a person holding it. Designs such as the Balfour and the Weitlaner have two arms with adjustable blades and a ratchet or screw to set the spread. It frees the assistant for other tasks. It needs interchangeable parts made to tolerance, good steel and sterilisation before use. A slipping ratchet or too much force crushes the tissue.

name: Surgical electrocautery
note: Monopolar and bipolar designs; cutting current vs coagulation; minimal tissue damage vs spark coagulation; safety protocols for anesthesia
_internal: [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

name: Surgical tourniquet
note: Bloodless field enables fine dissection; time limit critical to prevent tissue necrosis; cuff pressure above systolic; Esmarch exsanguination

name: Blood transfusion
note: Whole blood or separated components; indications for hemorrhage and anemia; citrate anticoagulation; compatibility testing beforehand

name: Blood typing and cross-matching
note: Landsteiner's groups; major and minor cross-match; agglutination reactions; hemolytic transfusion reactions from mismatch

name: Blood bank and storage
note: Donor screening and testing; refrigeration at 4 C; citrate anticoagulation; shelf life limitations; coordinated supply for emergencies

name: Citrate anticoagulation
note: Using sodium citrate to stop blood clotting. Citrate binds the calcium that the clotting cascade needs, so donor blood can be stored and transfused without clotting. It needs chemical purity and blood typing and cross-matching so the transfusion does not poison the patient. Massive transfusion can cause citrate poisoning, because the citrate removes calcium from the patient. It is later used in dialysis.

name: Intravenous saline solution
note: Isotonic with plasma; no hemolysis; replaces losses from hemorrhage and dehydration; colloid vs crystalloid later debated

name: Anaesthetic machine
note: Cylinders, regulators, flowmeters, vaporizer, carbon dioxide absorber, reservoir bag, mask and circuit; precise mixing prevents hypoxia

name: Endotracheal intubation
note: Direct vision with laryngoscope; cuffed tube prevents aspiration; IPPV with mechanical ventilation; complications from prolonged intubation

name: Spinal anaesthesia
note: Bier and Corning puncture; level of blockade; hypotension and bradycardia; post-dural puncture headache; advantages over general for lower surgeries

name: Local infiltration anaesthesia
note: Initial cocaine; later procaine and lidocaine; epinephrine added for vasoconstriction and prolonged effect; nerve blocks more selective

name: Appendicectomy
note: McBurney's point incision; ligation of appendicular artery; stump inversion; early diagnosis critical to prevent perforation and peritonitis

name: Hernia repair
note: Identification of defect; dissection of sac; return of viscera; fascial layer closure; recurrence common with simple suture alone

name: Gastrectomy
note: For ulcer or malignancy; Billroth I and II anastomoses; blood supply from left gastric, right gastric and gastroepiploic vessels

name: Caesarean section
note: Lower segment transverse vs classical vertical; classical not repeated in later pregnancies; perimortem indication when vaginal delivery not safe

name: Orthopaedic internal fixation
note: Fixing a broken bone from the inside with metal plates, screws and wires, so that the ends are held together and heal in place. Compression plating presses the fragments together. It needs interchangeable parts made to tolerance, metal that does not corrode in the body, and plaster casts for after-care. The hard parts are timing of when to move the limb, infection around the metal and delayed healing of the bone.

name: Plaster cast immobilization
note: Gypsum plaster bandage over clean padding immobilises a reduced fracture while it sets. Bone setting, swelling allowance, skin inspection, and keeping pressure off bony points are prerequisites.

name: Skeletal traction
note: Treating a broken bone by pulling steadily on the limb: a pin or wire is passed through the bone, and a rope with pulleys and weights pulls it. It is used for example for a broken thigh bone (femoral traction). It needs a drawn wire, a frame, pulleys and weights, and an understanding of the anatomy. The patient lies in bed for weeks, and skin care is critical to prevent sores.

name: Skin grafting
note: Full thickness vs split thickness; donor site must heal; vascularization of graft; autograft only option early; allograft rejection

name: Cataract extraction
note: An operation to remove the clouded lens of the eye. In the intracapsular method the lens is lifted out whole in its capsule; in the extracapsular method the capsule is left. The patient cannot focus afterwards (aphakia), so they are given thick glasses made of ground lenses to see. It needs delicate instruments and anatomical knowledge from dissection. Modern phacoemulsification came much later.

name: Thyroidectomy
note: Iodine preparation to reduce vascularity; recurrent laryngeal nerve identification; hypoparathyroidism from inadvertent gland removal; thyroid storm crisis

name: Digitalis glycosides
note: Withering's empirical observation; positive inotropic and negative chronotropic; narrow therapeutic window; digitalis toxicity from accumulation

name: Morphine isolation
note: Morphine, the main painkilling alkaloid of the opium poppy, first isolated in crystalline form by Serturner. Pure crystals give a measured dose, unlike raw opium, which varies. It can be taken by mouth or injected. It needs chemical extraction and analysis. The danger is that it slows breathing in overdose and is highly addictive.

name: Quinine isolation
kb: Alkaloid from cinchona bark for malaria
note: Pelletier and Caventou isolation; crystal form; bitter taste led to tonic water; cinchonism from high doses; synthetic substitutes later developed

name: Salicylate and aspirin
note: Salicylate, a painkilling and fever-reducing substance. Willow bark has been used traditionally; chemists isolated salicin, turned it into salicylate, and then acetylated it (added an acetyl group) to make aspirin, which is easier on the stomach. It needs plant chemistry and chemical analysis. It also thins the blood, an effect discovered later, so it may cause bleeding.

name: Barbiturate sedatives
note: Barbital, phenobarbital, pentobarbital; intravenous and oral; dependence and withdrawal; narrow margin between sedation and respiratory depression

name: Insulin extraction
note: Banting and Best 1921; pancreatic extract; purification; potency standardization in units; subcutaneous injection; insulin shock therapy

name: Thyroid hormone extract
note: A treatment made from dried thyroid glands of animals, given to people whose own thyroid fails. Later, synthetic thyroxine replaced it. Without the means to measure the hormone in blood, dosing is by symptoms, and the potency of the extract varies from batch to batch. It needs knowledge of the endocrine glands and hormones.

name: Adrenaline isolation
note: Takamine 1901 isolation; synthetic by 1906; cardiac and vascular effects; hypertensive crisis; added to local anesthetics for vasoconstriction

name: Sulphonamide drugs
note: Domagk's work; competitive antagonism of para-aminobenzoic acid; Prontosil red dye prodrug; broad spectrum but streptococcal resistance

name: Penicillin cultivation
note: Penicillium notatum on culture plates; broth fermentation; antibiotic activity in filtrate; scaling to deep tank fermentation

copy_visibility_reason: The brown liquor and the tank say nothing of the mould strain, the medium or the aeration; the wartime American effort needed the strain and the process shared from Britain.
name: Deep tank fermentation
note: Aeration and agitation; temperature and pH control; foaming control with silicone; corn steep liquor as nitrogen source; yield improvement over years

name: Freeze-drying penicillin
note: Vacuum and low temperature sublimation; water removal; stable powder form; reconstitution before injection; crystal structure preservation

name: Streptomycin isolation
note: Waksman's screening; first effective TB drug; ototoxicity and renal damage at high doses; resistance development in monotherapy

name: Antitoxin serum therapy
note: Serum from horses immunized with toxin. Diphtheria antitoxin reduced mortality from 50% to 20%. Anaphylaxis kills 1 in 1000. Passive immunity is temporary.

name: Smallpox vaccine
note: Jenner's cowpox observation; lymph from pustule; arm-to-arm transfer; lyophilization for storage; eradication by vaccination

name: Rabies vaccine
note: Pasteur's rabies vaccine, made from the dried nerve tissue of infected animals so that the germ is weakened. Because rabies takes weeks to reach the brain, the vaccine is given as a series of injections after the bite, and timing is critical: it must start before symptoms appear, since there is no cure after. It needs animals, a sterile laboratory and knowledge of immunity.

name: Typhoid vaccine
note: Heat-killed or chemical inactivation; partial protection; revaccination needed; enteric fever still endemic in poor sanitation

name: Cholera vaccine
note: Killed phenol-treated organisms; mucosal immunity weak with injected vaccine; oral rehydration more life-saving than vaccination

name: Plague vaccine
note: Killed bacillus; variable efficacy; antiplague serum more immediately useful; vector control reduces need for vaccination

name: Diphtheria toxoid
note: Diphtheria toxoid: the poison made by the diphtheria germ is treated with formalin so that it is no longer harmful but still trains the body to fight it. This works better than a killed germ. A Schick test, a small skin injection of toxin, shows whether a person is already immune. It needs a laboratory that can grow the germ and formalin, and knowledge of immunity.

name: Tetanus toxoid
note: Formalin inactivation of toxin; effective but slower than antitoxin; booster doses maintain immunity; wound prophylaxis combination with antitoxin

name: Pertussis vaccine
note: Whole cell killed vaccine; high fever and local reaction; acellular vaccine much later; maternal antibodies in infant protection

name: Yellow fever vaccine
note: 17D strain attenuation; long-lived immunity; dengue and other flaviviruses cross-protect partially; vector control still needed

name: Vitamin A and deficiency
note: Night blindness and xerophthalmia from deficiency; provitamin A in beta-carotene; hypervitaminosis A toxicity; fortification of milk

name: Vitamin B1 thiamine
note: Thiamine, vitamin B1, whose lack causes beriberi, a disease of nerves and heart. The vitamin is found in rice bran and in whole grain, so polished white rice eaters fall ill. There are wet and dry forms of the disease; in heavy drinkers a related brain disorder (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) appears. It needs chemical analysis and an experiment on diet to show the cause.

name: Vitamin B12 cobalamin
note: Pernicious anemia from intrinsic factor deficiency; injected when oral absorption fails; only animal source; methylmalonuria in deficiency

name: Vitamin C ascorbic acid
note: Ascorbic acid, vitamin C, whose lack causes scurvy: bleeding gums, weakness and wounds that do not heal. Citrus and fresh fruits and vegetables supply it. A deficiency also impairs the body's response to infection. It needs chemical analysis. The practical challenge is to carry fresh sources on long voyages, since the vitamin is lost by cooking and storage.

name: Vitamin D cholecalciferol
note: Vitamin D, whose lack causes rickets, a disease in which children's bones stay soft and bend. Cod liver oil is a rich source, and sunlight acting on the skin makes it. A deficiency also upsets the body's calcium control (secondary hyperparathyroidism). It needs chemical analysis. Cities with smoky skies and children kept indoors are at risk.

name: Iodised salt
note: Table salt with a small amount of an iodine compound added, to prevent goitre, the swelling of the thyroid gland that arises in regions where the soil and water lack iodine. It needs knowledge of the thyroid and a salt supply. The iodine slowly degrades with time and moisture, and whether people accept the fortified salt varies from culture to culture.

name: Oral rehydration solution
note: A drink of clean water with measured amounts of glucose and salt, given by mouth to people with severe diarrhoea. Glucose helps the small intestine take up sodium and water together, so it works as well as a drip in a vein for most patients. The ratio of salt to sugar is critical: too little does not work and too much makes things worse. It needs clean water and weighing.

name: Sand filtration
note: Biofilm layer (schmutzdecke) removes particles and pathogens; slow rate; microorganism breakthrough possible; pre-treatment needed
_internal: [HEURISTIC: yearly upkeep taken as one percent of the construction labour hours (repair and keeping the works in service); no wear or failure model yet.] [GATE: Draws on a water supply that is built and kept in service; with the aqueduct shut there is no flow to treat, lift or distribute.]

name: Water chlorination
note: Free and combined chlorine; residual for distribution; trihalomethane formation from organic matter; hypochlorite solution easier than gas

name: Separate sewage collection
note: Building separate drains for foul sewage and for rain water, so that heavy storms do not flood sewers and overload the treatment plant. Combined systems are cheaper to build, but they overflow in rain and carry sewage into rivers. Rain also leaks into pipes (infiltration and inflow), which is a constant difficulty. It needs the existing sewers and aqueducts with water supply.
_internal: [HEURISTIC: yearly upkeep taken as one percent of the construction labour hours (repair and keeping the works in service); no wear or failure model yet.] [GATE: Takes its flow from, or is laid into, a sewer that is built and kept clear; with the sewer shut it has nothing to act on.]

name: Activated sludge treatment
note: Microorganism flocs oxidize organic matter; aeration essential; solids separation by settling; sludge recycling; process control critical
_internal: [HEURISTIC: yearly upkeep taken as one percent of the construction labour hours (repair and keeping the works in service); no wear or failure model yet.] [GATE: The sludge works treat the foul flow that separate collection delivers; without it there is nothing to aerate.]

name: Milk pasteurisation
note: Low-temperature long-time or high-temperature short-time; kills TB, brucella, campylobacter; spoilage organisms also reduced

name: Meat inspection
note: Inspecting animals and meat before sale, by looking and by feeling the organs for disease, to find tuberculosis, anthrax and trichinosis (a parasitic worm in pork). Condemned meat is destroyed, and the inspection is recorded. It needs trained inspectors, knowledge of anatomy from dissection and an authority with power to enforce the rules. Butchers resist because condemned meat is lost profit.

name: Food purity legislation
note: A law that defines what counts as an adulterant (a cheaper material mixed into food to cheat the buyer or even to poison them), sets food standards, requires labels, and punishes offenders. It needs chemical analysis to detect substitutes, inspectors and a court willing to enforce it. Without testing, the law is a dead letter; with it, honest sellers are protected.

name: Notifiable disease system
note: A system by which doctors must report certain diseases to the authorities as soon as they appear, so that outbreaks are noticed early and can be contained. It needs a vital registration system, a rapid way of reporting, and protections for the confidentiality of patients. It works only if doctors comply and if the authorities act on reports. New threats can be spotted quickly.

name: Contact tracing
note: Case finding and source identification; quarantine placement; cohort management; resource-intensive but effective for containment

name: Isolation hospital
note: Site isolation and water supply; large grounds for convalescence; design for natural ventilation; segregation by disease

hazard_counters.label: the sick kept apart from the well

disease_effects.label: the sick kept apart from the well

_internal: [HEURISTIC: yearly upkeep taken as one percent of the construction labour hours (repair and keeping the works in service); no wear or failure model yet.]

name: Vector control
note: Map disease against mosquitoes, fleas, or lice and remove breeding sites, isolate bedding, and install barriers. Chemical insecticides and resistance management are separate later technologies.

name: Mosquito bed net
note: Simple barrier; treated with insecticide for duration; major malaria control tool; high coverage critical for population effect

name: Improved pit latrine
note: A latrine in which a pit holds human waste, covered and ventilated, so that faeces are contained and cannot contaminate water or food, and a vent pipe lets odour out and keeps flies away. It needs digging, a lining and a lid. It is cheap and useful where there is no sewer. Pits placed too near a well pollute it, and full pits must be closed and moved.

name: Hospital infection control
note: The practices that stop infection spreading in a hospital: washing of hands, cleaning of rooms, isolating infectious patients, and sterilising instruments in an autoclave (a steam pressure vessel). It needs boiled water, an autoclave and, above all, trained staff who comply. The hard part is education and discipline, since a single lapse by one person can carry infection to many.

name: Maternal health clinic
note: Screening for hypertension and proteinuria; dietary advice; postpartum hemorrhage and infection prevention; early detection of problems

name: Child health clinic
note: Vaccination records; growth monitoring; disease surveillance; screening for developmental delay; accident prevention counseling

name: Case record keeping
note: A standard written record for each patient, in a fixed order: history, problem list, assessment and plan, and follow-up over time. It lets a second physician take over care, and it makes a measure of quality of care possible. It needs literate staff, paper or other writing material, and the habit of controlled observation. It is the basis of the later study of many cases together.

name: Case series analysis
note: A study that describes a number of patients with the same condition to identify a pattern and the natural course of the disease. It generates hypotheses and can be published rapidly. It has no control group, so it cannot show that a treatment caused an improvement; people may have got better on their own. It needs good case records and is the first rung of clinical study design.

name: Cohort study
note: Prospective or retrospective; relative risk calculation; attrition and confounding challenges; expensive but strong evidence

name: Case-control study
note: Odds ratio approximates relative risk; efficient for rare diseases; recall bias and selection bias risks; faster than cohort

name: Randomised controlled trial
note: Gold standard for efficacy evidence; eliminates selection bias; requires large sample sizes; protocol registration and monitoring critical

name: Blinding in trials
note: Single blind subject only, double blind subject and investigator, triple blind adds assessor; unblinding for safety; masked capsules and injections

name: Placebo control
note: Ethical constraints: cannot use placebo when proven treatment exists; placebo effect real but separate from pharmacological effect

name: Medical statistics
note: Hypothesis testing; confidence intervals; power calculations; multiple comparison corrections; tabulation by hand or machine

name: Mortality table
kb: Actuarial analysis of age-specific mortality for population
note: Life expectancy calculation; actuarial science; insurance basis; improved sanitation and childhood survival change tables markedly

name: Vital registration system
note: Legal proof of identity; cause of death requires physician; population denominator for rates; undercount in poor regions

name: Professional nursing
note: Nightingale training standards; apprenticeship in hospital; gender issues in recruitment; autonomy vs physician delegation

name: Cadaver dissection
note: Legal cadaver supply from executed criminals and unclaimed poor; religious objections; reveals anatomy without speculation

name: Medical licensing
note: Qualification standards; examination by peers; legal monopoly; disciplinary power; excludes charlatans but also innovation

name: Medical journal publication
note: Priority claims and knowledge dissemination; peer review for quality; citation tracking; reproducibility and fraud detection

name: Pharmacopoeia
note: Prescription reference; legal authority; assurance of composition and quality; updated as new drugs appear and old ones refined

name: Drug standardisation
note: Setting a measure of strength for medicines that cannot be weighed, such as insulin and antitoxin, by units of activity tested on animals. Natural products vary in strength from batch to batch, so a given dose may be too weak or poisonous. Animal tests (bioassay) compare each batch with a reference. It needs chemical analysis, animals and careful records.

name: Bioassay
note: Measuring the strength of a drug by its effect on living animals, because no chemical test exists yet. Reproducibility is the difficulty: animals differ, so careful statistical design is used to refine the test, which in turn reduces the number of animals needed compared with crude testing. It needs a colony of test animals, a reference preparation and drug standardisation.

name: Methylene blue staining
note: Staining microscope slides with methylene blue, a dye made from coal tar chemistry. It colours bacteria and white blood cells a vivid blue so they can be seen and counted. Variations of it underlie the Gram and acid-fast stains, which separate bacteria into groups. It was discovered by Ehrlich. It needs a synthetic dye industry and a microscope.

name: Spirometer
note: An instrument that measures how much air a person can breathe. The patient blows into a bell, which is dry or sealed in water, and the volume of air displaced is read on a scale. The pattern of breathing shows whether the lungs are obstructed (air cannot get out) or restricted (they cannot fill). It needs a thermometer-grade scale of fine metalwork and a bell light enough to move freely.

name: Surgical light source
note: A bright light for surgery and examination. Carbon arc lamps came first, giving strong light but with heat and fumes, and tungsten filament lamps came later. The reflector geometry concentrates light on the wound without shadows, and the colour temperature of the light affects how well tissue colours are judged. It needs electric power and arc or incandescent lamps. Heat must be kept off the patient and the surgeon.

name: Microbiology culture technique
note: Growing bacteria on agar in Petri dishes (shallow lidded glass dishes) so that each germ grows into a visible colony. The shape of the colonies, together with stains such as the Gram stain, identifies the germ, and the culture can be tested for sensitivity to antibiotics. It needs agar, sterile technique, an incubator and a microscope. Contamination from outside germs spoils plates.

name: Plant chemistry extraction
note: Extracting the active substances from medicinal plants. A solvent is chosen that dissolves the wanted compound, the solution is concentrated, and the compound is crystallised; its identity is checked and the final product standardised. It needs a condenser for distilling spirits and essential oils, and chemical analysis. The hard part is purity and consistency, since the strength of plant material varies.

name: Agar culture media
note: Agar is the whole point and it is not obvious: gelatin melts at blood heat and is digested by the very bacteria you are growing, so plates liquefy overnight. Agar from red seaweed sets at 40 C, melts at 85 C and almost nothing eats it, which is why solid plate culture works at all. Red seaweed (Gelidium and relatives) grows around most temperate and Mediterranean coastlines and is available wherever you have sea access to them.
